title: Position of adjectives
subtitle: the high price / the price seemed high
summary: Decide whether an adjective goes before its noun, after a linking verb, or immediately after the noun.

lesson.heading: Two possible positions

right.label: After a linking verb (appear, be, become, feel, get, seem)

lesson.note: Many adjectives work in both positions - but a good number do not.

lesson.heading: 'a-' adjectives stay after the verb
lesson.text: Adjectives beginning with a- are seldom or never used before the noun. Several of them have a related adjective that can go before a noun.

examples.text: The horse was **alone** in the field.
The animal was **alive**. / A **living** animal. / A **live** animal.
He stood at the bedroom door, looking at his **sleeping** daughter.

lesson.note: Also afraid, alike, ashamed, awake, aware. Pairs: afraid - frightened, alike - similar, alone - lone, asleep - sleeping.

lesson.heading: Health and feelings
lesson.text: Adjectives describing health and feelings normally come after a linking verb. They are sometimes used between an adverb and a noun.

examples.text: She spent most of her life nursing **seriously ill** children in the hospital.
examples.note: an adverb makes ill possible before the noun

lesson.note: Also content, fine, glad, sorry, (un)sure, upset, well. Some fixed uses do come before a noun: ill health, an upset stomach, He's really not a well man.

lesson.heading: Emphasising, classifying and qualitative adjectives
rows: Emphasising: complete, absolute, entire, mere, sheer, total, utter
It was a **total** failure. / I felt a **complete** fool.
Classifying: nuclear, atomic, chemical, digital, domestic, environmental, medical, general, occasional, northern, maximum, underlying
seldom: ~~The explosion was nuclear~~, unless we particularly want to contrast it with other kinds of explosion
lesson.note: Some classifying adjectives have a different, qualitative meaning after a linking verb: the country's **economic** reforms and The process isn't **economic**. (= not profitable). Also academic, conscious, educational, (il)legal, scientific.

lesson.heading: Immediately after the noun
lesson.text: Many adjectives can start a reduced relative clause straight after a noun - especially when the adjective is followed by a to-infinitive or a prepositional phrase.

examples.text: It was a speech **calculated to appeal** to the unions.
He is a manager **capable of making** difficult decisions.
As the minister **responsible for** the health service, I think he should resign.

lesson.heading: -ible and -able adjectives
lesson.text: Adjectives like available, imaginable, possible and suitable go straight after the noun only when the noun follows the, or when a following relative clause makes the noun definite.

examples.text: This was the most difficult decision **imaginable**.
It is a treatment **suitable for** all children with asthma.
It's the only room **available** in the hotel that night.

lesson.heading: concerned, present, responsible

left.label: Immediately after the noun
examples: All the people **present** (= who were there) approved of the decision.
The party was excellent, and I'd like to thank all the people **concerned**. (= who were involved)
As the minister **responsible** for the health service ... (= who is in charge of it)

right.label: Before the noun
examples: I was asked for my **present** address. (= my address now)
Cars drive too fast past the school and **concerned** parents have complained. (= worried)
Children are only admitted when accompanied by a **responsible** adult. (= sensible, trustworthy)

lesson.note: Also involved, opposite, proper: the **opposite** effect (= the reverse), the people **involved** (= who took part).

exercises.statement: We were unsure which way to go.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Unsure describes a feeling, so it belongs after a linking verb - exactly where it is.

exercises.prompt: In the distance I could see ___ figure walking towards me.
exercises.explanation: Alone is not used before a noun; the related adjective lone is.

exercises.prompt: The fire on the ship is under control, but there are still many ___ passengers on board.
exercises.explanation: Afraid cannot go before a noun, so we use frightened instead.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence with the version that puts the adjective before the noun.

pairs.left: The horse was alone in the field.
The two children were alike in age.

exercises.statement: She spent most of her life nursing seriously ill children in the hospital.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Ill can come before a noun when there is an adverb in front of it, as in a terminally ill patient.

exercises.statement: It wasn't a great surprise when Rahim died as he hadn't been a well man for years.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Well normally follows a linking verb, but 'a well man' is an established exception, usually in the negative.

exercises.prompt: After Dr Owen left the project, its failure was ___.
exercises.explanation: Utter is an emphasising adjective, so it is not used after a linking verb.

exercises.prompt: The computer fault was ___ enough to disrupt all the work in the office.
exercises.explanation: Underlying is a classifying adjective and only goes before a noun (the underlying problem).

exercises.prompt: None of the equipment in the warehouse is ___.
exercises.explanation: Domestic classifies the equipment, so it isn't normally used after a linking verb.

exercises.prompt: The party was excellent, and I'd like to thank ___.
exercises.explanation: After the noun, concerned means 'who were involved'; before the noun it means 'worried'.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order. The speaker is talking about the minister in charge of the health service.
exercises.answer: As the minister responsible for the health service, I think he should resign.
exercises.explanation: Responsible + for is part of an adjective phrase, so it follows the noun.

exercises.prompt: Where can each adjective normally be used?
